Before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I wish to call the attention of the Prime Minister to a statement which he made in the House that he would bring down a statement as to why certain voters' lists had not been printed. I have before me the voters' list for Sunbury and Queen's for 1904, and I have not yet had any voters' list for my constituency for 1903. I think this is unfair treatment. I understand that this means that two voters' lists have been got out for New Brunswick since 1 have had any.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to refer to an apparent discourtesy on my part to the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram). Yesterday afternoon by a previous arrangement, I paid a visit to a very interesting object lesson in connection with the agricultural estimates in the shape of live stock and other attractions. While there I witnessed exhibitions of high tumbling, but had no idea that we were going to have any exhibition of low tumbling in this House. In the evening at seven fifty, I came into the House to get my letters. I did not open them all at the moment, but went to an interesting social function and it was only after eleven o'clock that I found among them a courteous invitation from my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), inviting me to be present in the afternoon as he proposed to revive the discussion of the matter in controversy between us. Had I known this earlier, I would have been present yesterday afternoon, and have put aside the arrangement I had made. I am not aware however that he lost much by my absence, because in any event I would not have replied to the observations which the hon. gentleman made. I wish to avoid as far as

possible any personal controversy with anybody. I do not challenge or attack anybody, and on several occasions have avoided encounters, though perhaps it was my duty to have met them. The reason why I did not wish to have any controversy with my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), is because I am afraid of him, for I think that to some slight extent he was in the right. But I had other reasons for not wishing to meet my hon. friend from Bast Elgin. I am afraid of my hon. friend physically, intellectually and morally. And further, I am afraid of myself ; and do not wish to make in this House any exhibiton of temper whatever. When I do, I am sorry afterwards, because X prefer not to say or do anything which will leave an unpleasant feeling. So far as the observations of my hon. friend from Lennox are concerned, I merely spoke from memory, and I am quite willing to offer any reparation, if unintentionally I have done him any injury. I hope to continue to enjoy the friendship of my hon. friend. We occasionally exchange some words of banter, but are usually on the best of relations, which I trust will continue. But with regard to the observations of my hon. friend from Bast Elgin, I cannot make the same free admission. I did not refer to him either directly or by imputation, yet he volunteered a personal attack upon myself. He attempted to convict me of an untruth and of having had my views coloured by the fact that I am an agent of the Hamburg-American Line. On the latter point, let me say that whenever I have spoken, I have taken pains to openly state that it was in consequence of my connection with that line that I was in a position to obtain information and consequently could speak from personal knowledge. The hon. gentleman, however, was very anxious to accuse me of having stated what was an untruth, and as there were a number of people in the House and the galleries at the time, he made his charge as conspicuously as possible. ' Hansard ' in hand he made this statement without any reservation or qualification.
I would remind the Junior member for Halifax (Mr. William Roche) that he is mistaken when he thinks that the hon. member for Lennox followed him last year with his speech or even with a speechlet. There is no record of either such speech or speechlet. But I can tell him that the hon. gentleman who did follow him and who criticised his language very severely was the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver).
Hear, hear.

I shall now quote from page 6610 of last year's ' Hansard ' to show what did take place and what is recorded. The Minister of the Interior said:
The only persons we hear that suggestion from is the hon. member for Lennox and his friend the United States inspector, Mr. Watchorn. If my understanding of the hon. gentleman's argument is correct, it is in effect Mr. WM. ROCHE.
that we should make such an arrangement as would allow the officers of the United States to decide who should come into Canada.

I made no such statement. What I said was that we ought to enter into an arrangement with' them, that we ought to have as much to say about it as the Americans, and that there should be a good understanding between the two governments.
That brought up the whole question as to the strictness of the inspection by our Canadian officers. The Minister of the Interior went on to say :
They are all presided over by a general inspector of first-class professional attainments; and we have no reason whatever to believe that it is necessary that their inspection should be revised by officers of the United States.
That was in the same debate and in pursuance of the same controversy. The hon. member for Lennox then said :
When was the medical inspector appointed at Montreal ?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the date.

I may say that his deputy minister was before the committee as late as the 11th of June, and, according to his evidence, no one had been appointed there then.
There are three instances of the hon. gentleman from Lennox making short speeches and yet the hon. member for East Elgin says there is no record of his having made any speeches or speechlets after mine.
They had no reference to you at all.

Without any reservation, equivocation or limitation he wanted to make a direct attack, and he made a positive statement there were none and he shall not wriggle out of it. Now, on the same evening there was another debate on the question of salaries and appropriations on the same subject, and during the course of that my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) made five short speeches. That is sufficient. I was only speaking from memory and only reciting what was my impression at the time, for I had no opportunity of consulting the record or refreshing my memory- Now I want to say that I do not appear in this House as a gladiator by any means ; I do not want to enter the lists in competition with my hon. friend. Now and hereafter he may say what he likes and do what he likes with reference to myself ; I shall not reply to any personal observations. But if at any time anything is said affecting the interests of my constituents that seems to me to call for a word from me, I' shall take the opportunity of replying.
On this question that what really troubles my hon. friend is the truth ; and on this subject his conscience smites him, for once at any rate. In this case he was clearly in the wrong. He spoke without full investigation of the subject and made a flamboyant speech hoping that I would not take notice

of it and that it would pass as a refutation of what X had said. If he thinks he is equipped and qualified to enter into competition with those who engage in personalities, who are apt to fling back recrimination for recrimination, and to bandy comparisons perhaps as expressive as his own or indulge in any scurrility, he may find that there are people of that kind who will meet him and transfix him, when he will be dead as a smelt.

I have only a word or two to say in reply to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche). If a man is to be attacked, at least he can prepare for the attack if he has reasonable notice. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) in this matter, .has not done me the courtesy of giving me 'fair warning. When I intended to speak of him yesterday I gave him due notice. He read my letter and though he replied also by letter which was sent to me last night at eleven o'clock, he did not have the courtesy to say in that letter that he was going to make another attack on me to-day. This is the hon. gentleman's letter to me :
Ottawa, 2nd June, 1904.
11 p.m.

Ingram, Esq.,
House ofCommons.
Sir,-I have just opened your letter. Had I received it in time, I might have put aside a previous engagement, hut, was out of town this afternon.
I am, dear sir.
Your most obedient servant,

It would not have hurt my hon. friend to ndd a postscript that he intended to bring up this matter this afternoon. The hon. gentleman must be afaid, however, as he admits, or his conscience must have troubled him- something must have been the matter when lie was not willing to give me the British fair play that I offered him yesterday ? I Ho not think there is anything to reply to in what the hon. gentleman has said. The statement I made is unanswerable. I am willing to let the record stand. If anything can be established which shows that my statement was in any way wrong, I am willing to apologize. But I am quite satisfied that I shall never be called upon to .apologize because my statements are absolutely correct. As to entering into personalities, I can tell the hon, gentleman that there is not in my statement a single word of a personal character-not one.

Had the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) [DOT]dropped this subject the first day, he would never have heard of it from me, because so far as I know, he and I have been upon the best terms in this House.
But you will never speak as you pass by, after this.

Oh, yes. If the hon. gentleman holds the feeling that he expresses, we shall be good friends yet. I wish to say that there was not a single interruption of any kind when the hon. gentleman was speaking on this subject a year ago, nor did I say anything with reference to what he had stated. My interruptions were entirely in the speech of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). Several members had spoken between my speech and that of the junior member for Halifax. When the Minister of the Interior spoke, he seemed to me to put woi'ds into my mouth that I had not uttered, and I told him. So far as I am concerned I want no personalities. I have no feeling in the matter, and the only thing that surprised me was that the junior member for Halifax should bring the question up a second time. He has now brought it up a third time. So far as I am concerned, let it drop where it is.

speechtext: I am sorry to say I must again tell my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) that I cannot answer his question. The Postmaster 'General (Sir) William Mulock) is away. I expected him this morning, but he has not yet returned. When he returns I shall be able to answer.

Before the Orders of the Day are called I desire to ask the Minister of Trade and

Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) for information with regard to tenders for the steamship service between British Columbia and Mexico. 'The Daily Times' of Victoria, an organ of the government, a few days ago, published the following :
In the preliminary agreement made between Canada and Mexico in connection with the steamship service for which tenders are being called, it is provided that Victoria or any other port where business offers will be a port of call for the vessels of the line. This provision of the agreement will also be inserted in the contract with the steamship company.
Now, I understand that in the call for tenders no' provision is made for these steamers calling at the city of Victoria, and I would like to ask the minister if it is intended that that shall be inserted ?

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT (Minister of Trade and Commerce).
speechtext: Generally speaking, in these contracts we have a clause allowing the minister to direct the calls to be made. In any case it is intended to have a clause inserted by which the steamships shall call at Victoria.
On their Inward and outward voyages?
Both.

I would like to make a brief reference to the same subject, on the Atlantic and not on the Pacific side. I notice that in the tenders which are called for the steamship service between Canada and Mexico on the Atlantic side, the port of St. John in entirely omitted. There is no mention made that St. John shall be a port of call for the service. I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether St. John is to be entirely excluded from this service or not. I have no doubt in the world that, if St. John were made a port of call there would be a very considerable trade between that port and Mexico to which this steamship service will go. I would like to hear from the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to that matter.

For
these matters the amount of money at our disposal is not very large, and I am not quite in a position to say whether we will be able to deal with both services. But I think I will be able to meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman.
Are any negotiations going on now respecting the establishment of a fast Atlantic line, and if so, what stage have they reached ?
No negotiations other than the additional contract that was laid on the table with the Allan's, and which the hon. gentleman has seen. It was laid on the table some time ago.
Then the whole thing is over ?
I do not say that, but no negotiations are going on at the present moment.
Has the minister any data as to the business to be carried on by these steamers between Canada and Mexico ? I presume some reports have been made as to the nature of the trade that can be worked up.
The report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for January supplies the information he requires.
Are these steam-, ers going to call at any other port ?
We will see what we can do. The money at our disposal is not very large. I do not know yet what arrangements we will be able to make.

House in Committee of Supply.
Quarantine-salaries and contingencies of organized districts and public health in other districts, $150,000.
Explain.

The committee will notice that there is a very considerable decrease in the amount asked for. I am glad to say that this is due to the fact that the necessary precautions against the introduction of small-pox from the United States seem to be at an end ; in fact, the danger is at an end although there is here and there some expenditure on that account. Last year 1 was obliged to ask for a considerable sum of money to deal with the frontier, and also to deal with some outbreaks of small-pox in our own Northwest. These outbreaks have practically disappeared and I trust that the cycle of years during which this danger from small-pox has been imminent has passed away and that for several years we will not be obliged to spend as large a sum of money on this account as formerly. The expenditure in connection with quarantine is the same as it has been for several years past.
How much money was expended last year on some of the different items ?

Last year we spent on public health generally, which covers the head office and some salaries, $9,000 odd. Along the American frontier we spent $28,644. And the Northwest Territorial accounts amounted % to $22,000 odd, making a total of $60,000 odd. * I am speaking in round numbers. At the Halifax quarantine we spent $9,000, at Sydney nearly $4,000, at Pictou, $300, at Grosse Isle, Quebec, nearly $40,000, at St. John.N.B. $11,500, at Chatham, N.B., $730, at Charlottetown, P.E.I., $1,564, at Vancouver, $800, and at Victoria, N.B., $17,900, making a total of $145,000 odd.

I notice in the Auditor General's Report, page D-53, in connection with the quarantine service at St. John, an amount of $200 for horse-hire. It is impossible for the quarantine officer at St. John to require a horse for his use unless such horse is like the ancient Pegasus, and is provided with wings because he could only get down to Partridge Island by water. Therefore, it puzzles me very much indeed to know what this amount of $200 for horse-hire means. I also noticed in connection with the public accounts committee that the department had purchased a wagon and harness which were receipted for by the same officer and which are stated to be necessary for the proper carrying out of the service. The quarantine officer there has an allowance, I understand, for boat-hire, so that he
may be taken to and fro in the discharge of his duty, but what use he has for a horse I cannot conceive at all unless it is to go fishing or something of that kind. Certainly I think that item should be fully explained. If it is the intention of the department to raise the salary of that officer by that amount of $200 I have nothing to say against it whatever, but I do think that an item of this kind should be fully explained. I cannot conceive what it is for.

The explanation is a very simple one. The wharf is a distance from the hospital and the detention building and sick people who are landed and have to be kept in quarantine have to be taken from the wharf with their luggage and effects to the hospital. There is a horse there for that purpose and a wagon and harness are also provided. There is no possibility df the doctor in charge using his horse for pleasure purposes because the island has only an area of a few acres on which no driving could be done. The horse is never taken away from the island.
The horse is kept on the island ?	-
Certainly.
At what time is the horse taken to the island ?
I think the horse has been there for several years ; or at all events a horse has been there for several years. I do not know whether that particular horse has or not.

I notice a large amount of expenditure in the Northwest Territories and I would like an explanation from the hon. minister in reference to some of this expenditure. He will find the accounts at page D-63 of the Auditor General's Report. The first item is that of Dr. James Patterson, of Winnipeg, who has charged for 250 days at $20 a day with travelling and living expenses amounting to $1,196.77. This seems to me a very large amount of money to pay to this gentleman living in Winnipeg for overseeing the quarantine stations in the Northwest Territories. The travelling expenses must have been increased to this amount because of the fact that the gentleman lived in Winnipeg and not up in the Territories themselves. I have looked at the report of this gentleman and of all the items which I see included in the report of the department, his is the most meagre and contains the least information. But the point to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister is the question of the necessity in this part of the service which belongs more especially to the interior of the country of an officer of this kind. I can understand that the service up there needs a head of some kind, but if you look over the report

of the Auditor General for the Northwest Territories you find that at points where small-pox existed, some forty doctors were employed, looking after the patients and all of these were paid out of that $24,028. About $15,000 was paid to the medical staff for these cases. On page D-67 there is an item.
Rush, W. T. M.D., attendance, vaccinating, quarantining, &c., July 31st to October 1, 1902, $301.95.
That applies to all the duties connected with these people, and if you go over the report you will find that the same thing occurred in many places. Go to Whitewood. and you will see that Dr. James Budd is credited with establishing quarantine sixty miles, $65. Then go to Oxbow, and there is an item :

, M.D.: medical services, 37 days' attendance at quarantine station at $10 ; 5 visits to country at $12.50 ; team, 5 days at $5 ; telegrams, $2.35 ; medicine, $5-$464.
Thus I cannot possibly see where the services of Dr. Patterson, of Winnipeg, came in, although he was paid in all about $6,000 for these 250 days' service.
I do not wish to say anything in criticism of the charges, but there seems to be no system at all, because, if we take the case of Dr. Smith, at Medicine Hat. we find that he vaccinated twenty-nine people at $1 for each person, and Dr. Calder, at the same place, vaccinated 230 people at 25 cents each. Of course, Dr. Calder is very moderate ; I am not objecting to the charges at all, but it seems strange that in one case you pay 25 cents and in another you pay $1. At Duck Lake we find Dr. Stewart vaccinating 250 half-breeds at 50 cents each. That is. a wholesale contract, I suppose. Dr. Smyth then vaccinated twenty-nine patients at $1 each, and Dr. Calder vaccinated 230 at 25 cents each. Dr. Calder was very moderate in all his charges. He travelled 56 miles at 50 cents a mile. He apparently had not then understood that he was in the employ of the government.
The point to which I want to draw attention is that all this work was done at the expense of this country. When these people were unfortunate enough to contract small-pox a medical man was sent to them at once, and all the expenses were paid by the country. In the report of the Minister of the Interior you will see that if immigrants coming into this country are unfortunate enough to be quarantined for any cause whatever, they have to pay their own expenses or be deported with their families back to the country from which they came. I cannot see the justice of making that distinction between two classes of people. It may be that some agent has persuaded an emigrant to come to this country. He may be a poor man with a family of four or five, who comes here with very little money, Mr. VROOMAN.
and may contract some contagious disease upon the boat, perhaps from some one on board or from rats on the ship. Such a man lands here and has no money to pay expenses and he is sent to his home. But up in the Northwest Territories, men who have lived there for years, and who may be in very easy and comfortable circumstances, are unfortunate enough to contract smallpox, the people of this country have to pay the expenses all the way through. I would like the minister to give an explanation of that.

I am very glad to give my hou. friend the information, and I am sure that he is not making these remarks in any spirit of captious criticism, but is simply seeking for information. I shall take up these questions in reverse order. My hon. friend spoke of the expenditure in this department being different from what it is in the Department of the Interior, and also referred to the fact that we make such expenditures in the Northwest Territories. In the Northwest Territories the Dominion has practically to pay the expenses which, in the organized provinces, are borne by the provincial treasury. It is a question, of course, in some cases whether that expenditure should be by a direct vote of this parliament or whether it should be taken out of the lump sum which this parliament votes to the territorial administration for its general administration. The principle has been that what has been that what is an annual charge there year after year should be provided for in a general way by a lump sum which this parliament would vote to the territorial administration for what I might call their territorial disbursements. In the case, however, of public health, and especially in the case of a small-pox epidemic, we have an unusually heavy expenditure, one which has happened to be large in the last year or two, but which I trust may not be at all large this year and may entirely disappear. In these circumstances, it is felt that the gov-eminent, through the department of quarantine and public health, must pay charges in the Territories just as a provincial government, through its boards of health and public health department, would pay the charges in a province.
The expenditure which my hon. friend is discussing is just such as a provincial government would make. The people who have been helped in these small-pox outbreaks are not well-to-do people. If expenses have been incurred for them, it is because they have been in indigent circumstances, and this being a contagious disease, it is necessary in the interests of the community that it should be dealt with by proper officials, and not by private practitioners. For this reason we have been doing there just such work as the provincial health authorities would do in a province. In the prov-

ince of Ontario the provincial board of health has done a very large amount of work in connection with outbreaks of smallpox during the last two or three years. My hon. friend has spoken of Dr. Patterson. I may say that Dr. Patterson was chosen as being a most competent man to have general charge of all this work. My hon. friend can easily understand that in such a sparsely settled country as the Northwest Territories, it would not do to trust the work entirely to local men. Very frequent-Iv there would be no local man within many miles of the actual case. Then, we might have reports from local men indicating an alarming state of affairs, which on invest! gation might prove to be not so alarming All through our quarantine work it has been proven necessary to have some independent oversight over the local men. It is quite impossible for the director general of public health at Ottawa to take this oversight, and for that reason Dr. Patterson was chosen. It might have been possible to get a man at Regina or some othei central point in the Territories ; but Dr Patterson was considered to possess in an eminent degree the necessary capacity and prestige for the work. The only difference Is the slight difference of railway fare when Dr. Patterson is obliged to go to the Territories, though in many instances the journey from Winnipeg would be easier than the journey from Regina or Medicine Hat. The mode of procedure is this. When an outbreak is reported, it is Dr. Patterson's duty either to go himself and investigate it, or to appoint some local man in whom he has confidence and on whose judgment he can relv, to investigate it and report. In many instances Dr. Patterson has had to go and make the investigation. He has found perhaps only one case. He has taken steps to isolate that, and has appointed a physician within convenient reach to look after it and see that the disease does not spread. In other cases, in which a number of people would be affected, a regular quarantine may have to be etablished for the community or for a number of houses. Dr. Patterson's travelling has been for the purpose of holding these investigations. His work has been paid for by the day, because it was work of a temporary character. I did not wish to appoint Dr. Patterson or anybody else as a permanent officer in the Territories at a fixed salary. It happens that the payment last year reached a very considerable sum. I am told that there are very few cases in the Territories at present, that the outbreak is practically over, and therefore I trust that the expenditure this year will be very slight indeed, and next year there may be no expenditure of this character at all. But Dr. Patterson's work has been most efficient and acceptable to the people; he has avoided any friction among the people, and has been able to prevent any serious spread of the disease.
My hon. friend has spoken of the different charges for vaccination, in some cases twenty-five cents in others fifty cents and in others a dollar a case. The difference depends entirely upon the nature of the conditions. If a man bas a couple of hundred people to vaccinate in a particular locality, he will naturally charge only twenty-five cents. If he has to go fifty miles to vaccinate a few people, he may have to charge more.

A larger mileage.
. Mr. FISHER. We would have to charge mileage for his travelling expenses, but at the same time he would have to spend considerable time in order to vaccinate a few people. I am informed and have noted in my departmental work that Dr. Patterson s accounts have been very carefully prepared. They have been sent here only after he has carefully examined and initialled them; and I am told by the accountant of the department that these accounts are among the best and most carefully prepared accounts that we have in the department. I understand that Dr. Patterson has a reputation from which we might expect that, and I am glad to know that that is the opinion of the chief accountant and the director general of public health in the department. I think my hon. friend will understand from this explanation that this work is being done in as practical and businesslike a way as possible, under the circumstances, the outbreaks having been very scattered, the distances great and the population sparse.

I would like to ask the minister where the vaccine which is used in these cases is obtained, whether in Canada or in the United States ? I believe there are places in Canada where vaccine is manufactured ; and that being so,' if it is as good a quality as can be obtained anywhere else, it should certainly have the preference.
I am informed that Dr. Patterson gets his vaccine at Regina from a firm known as the Canada Drug Company. I do not know where they get it.

I would like to ask the minister whether his department or the government have considered the propriety of establishing a department of public health for the Dominion ? I see by the report of the director general of public health that there is a resolution from the Canada Medical Association recommending that. I would like to know how the government looks upon it.

No decision has been reached. There are certain constitutional difficulties that might arise if the government should take action. Some people consider that it comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The matter is one well

worthy of consideration, which I have brought to the attention of my colleagues.

There is a question in connection with the quarantine, with regard to Manitoba, which I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. minister. I have bad a couple of communications from the secretary of the Provincial Board of Health in that province complaining of the manner in which the quarantine regulations are enforced. Knowing nothing personally about the matter, I shall' simply read the correspondence :
Winnipeg, May 11th, 1904. Dear Sir,-For some time past the Dominion government have made the pretense of appointing quarantine officers at certain points in southern Manitoba for the purpose of preventing small-pox from coming into the province. Two of these officials are Dr. Sharpe, of Morden, and Dr. Riddell, of Crystal City, and, I believe, there are others. These officials have regularly drawn their salaries for the past two or three years from the Dominion government, and there is scant evidence as to any value having been received for the expenditure. You can readily understand how inadequate and unproductive such an expenditure would be, by the medical men referred to being located at points far removed from the boundary line.
Some time ago I was advised, after making due inquiries, by the secretary of the State Board of Health of North Dakota, as to the prevalence to a very large extent of small-pox in the vicinity of St. John and Rolla, N.D.; in fact, the disease has been evident in this locality for the past year or two, and whether it is owing to inadequate quarantine provisions by the state authorities of North Dakota, the fact remains that the disease does not appear to be under control or on the wane.
At the present time there are upwards of 70 cases of small-pox in quarantine at St. Johns. This condition of affairs was brought by me to the attention of Dr. Montizambert, director general of public health, Ottawa, some few weeks ago, with the request that proper steps be taken by the appointment of persons along the boundary line to prevent persons from the infected district coming into Manitoba, to which a reply was received that Dr. Riddell, of Crystal City, had been requested to visit St. Johns and report. This report was received by Dr. Montizambert, who communicated the same to me, and was to the effect that about 68 cases of small-pox were in quarantine at St. Johns, but I have not been informed up to the present time, as to what, if any, action has been taken to prevent infected persons coming into the province, although I have requested Dr. Montizambert to so advise me on two or three occasions.
The most grevious complaint which the hoard has to make is that during the past month not a few cases have been allowed to come into the province from the infected district. The disfease first made its appearance at a place named Lundar, in the municipality of Posen, east of Lake Manitoba, of which you doubtless know the residents are principally composed of half-breeds. When informed as to the outbreak I wrote to one of the pro-Mr. FISHER.
minent men at that point asking the source of infection, who replied as follows
' I find that a few weeks hack a family from the states (Turtle Mountain district, I believe) moved in there, and that the infection came from them."
Dr. Cleghorn, one of the health officers of the municipality of Argyle, writes of the existence of four cases in the Rock Lake country, in the municipality of Argyle. He says [DOT] the infection was brought in by one John Bell, who had been visiting at St. Johns, N.D. Bell had been in quarantine in the St. Johns district, which district was then, and is now, I believe, infected with small-pox.'
Dr. Morrison, of Belmont, the other health officer for the municipality of Argyle, states that four cases have made their appearance in the district south of Belmont. The first ease came from North Dakota. The cases are amongst the half-breeds.'
Dr. Parr, health officer for the village of Morden, reports the existence of a case at Morden, having come from township 1 in range 7, being in the municipality of Pembina, and that the infection came into this section from across the line, and that persons have been, and are being permitted to cross the line with perfect impunity.
Another ground of complaint that the board has reason to make is that about a month ago certain Scotch emigrants were brought into the province by the Dominion government, and small-pox having made its appearance among one of their number, all were quarantined near the Louise bridge in St. Boniface. It appears that at Sudbury a number of Ontario settlers were put into this car along with the Scotch emigrants, and were quarantined along with thorn at St. Boniface, having been exposed to the infection. These Scotch emigrants were kept in quarantine the proper regulation period, but the Ontario settlers were allowed tlioir liberty, after being detained four or five days, and the result of this stupidity, on the part of the Dominion medical officer and immigration commissioner here, was, that these peopl.. were allowed to depart to all portions of the province. The first evidence of this most reprehensible proceeding on the part of rue Dominion authorities was that one of the passengers, Emory Valley, by name, went to Lauder and infected a whole family, which is now under quarantine at that point, and which will probably cost that municipality of Cameron several hundreds of dollars. This man Valley, after leaving the small-pox impression at Lauder, went to Brandon and wandered about the streets for several days, and then vanished, notwithstanding that the police and health officials of Brandon made all due endeavours to locate him. You will see therefore that the province has just grounds of complaint as to the action of the Dominion authorities in matters involving the administration of public health and the suppression of disease in this province.
You are aware, I have no doubt, that the province has no control or jurisdiction at the boundary line, and that it is necessary that any action taken at that point must be done by the Dominion authorities. What the province is entitled to expect, and should receive, is adequate protection in the premises, and I bring the foregoing facts to your attention for the purpose of giving publicity to the same

in the House as a representative from this province, with the object, if possible, that some live steps will be taken to protect the people of this province from the infection from outside points.
I regret to have to trouble you at such great length, but my justification is that the subject fully warrants the same. I will be pleased to hear from you at your earliest convenience.
Yours truly,
E. M. WOOD, Secretary.
Following that I received another letter, in which Mr. Wood complains very much of the scant courtesy paid these communications. He writes on May 13th :
Dear Sir,-Adverting, to the quarantine by the Dominion government along the southern boundary, I beg to say that on Saturday I received a telegram from Dr. Montizambert stating that medical frontier officers have been appointed and guards placed at points in the vicinity of Killarney, Deloraine, Morden and Crystal City. I am nevertheless of the opinion that it would do no harm if the matter was brought by you to the attention of the House.
I think you might also inquire as to the duties of the health officials who have been appointed as quarantine officers and guards at the points referred ; what they have been instructed to do, and how often it is intended that reports shall be received. The province is in great danger, if the order of things which has prevailed for some time past continues with having several epidemics of smallpox at points in the province.
Yours truly,

Secretary.
The complaint made by the secretary of the Provincial Board of Health is that in the first place the officials who were selected live at inland points, far removed from the boundary and consequently are not in a position to guard the boundary against the importation of disease. I understand that they draw $100 a month in addition to their regular practice, and the complaint is that they render no service for the money. He complains of the tardiness of the answer of his communications although admitting that, ou the 18th of May, when he writes, he had, at last received word that at several of these points officials had been placed. But he desires to know, and asks me to inquire on behalf of the province, what the duties of these officers are, also as to their reports, whether there is any stipulated time for these to be made, and generally, what duties are expected of these officers. The minister will recognize how important this matter is, especially now that the stream of immigration into that country is so great. It becomes now a most serious problem not only from a provincial standpoint because it will impose financial burdens upon the province. but because of the dangers to the people through the spread of these infectious diseases, and also because municipalities are likely to be put to large expense in taking charge of these patients.

I have no doubt the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. J. Roche) has confused two wholly different questions. One is that of guarding our frontier on the States, and the other is as to danger of importation of disease by immigrants who reach the west by train from eastern sea-board. X will refer to the latter first because it is the most easily disposed of. When immigrants come to the ports on the Atlantic? sea-board they must pass through the hands of our quarantine officers at GVosse Isle, St. John or Halifax. If these officials find no disease upon them, they allow them to enter the country. Our quarantine is a quarantine on the boundary or on the sea-board. After the immigrants pass that quarantine, my department has no more control over them anu no responsibility for them. They are then in the hands of the Immigration Department and are dealt with by that department. Of course this inspection cannot be absolutely perfect. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. .T. Roche) as a medical man, knows that it is impossible to provide a system of inspection which will enable us to detect infallibly the man who will afterwards develop a case of small-pox. As to the cases which are said to have come across the frontier from the United States, it is true that, in St. Johns, North Dakota there was an outbreak of small-pox. We were notified of that and took immediate steps to protect the frontier. Dr. Sharp was appointed at Morden, Dr. Riddell at Crystal City and Dr. Thornton at Deloraine, and Dr. White at Killarney. Dr. Sharp and Dr. Riddell were appointed a considerable time before Mr. Wood wrote to Dr. Montizambert and im-mediatelv on our discovery of the outbreak in St. Johns. It is true that Dr. Sharp and Dr. Riddell live at some distance from the boundary but they have a guard under them whose duty it is to watch the trail and every place of passage across the boundary. Of course, these guards are not medical men. It is impossible to get enough medical men to station one at every place where there is a trail across the frontier. You could not find the men, and, if yon could find them you could not pay them to stay and carry on this duty of watching, except at salaries which would be quite prohibitive. All we can do is to have the medical officer as near the frontier as possible and where he will be within reach when he is notified of any difficulty or danger. That has been the practice all through the country and it is the only course for us to follow. In a country like Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, where population is sparse and distances are considerable and where the frontier is an imaginary line with trails crossing it at many places, it is physically impossible to station a doctor at every point along the line or to have everybody who seeks to cross i medically examined by a doctor. The plan

we follow is to have a doctor as near as possible to the principle points, and, if necessary, allow him to employ guards to watch the trail along the means of communication as closely as possible. Then, where there is a case which arouses suspicion the doctor can be called in and make an examination. As a matter of fact this method has been generally successful. My hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) is aware that, even with every care, contagion may pass the boundary. I think my hon. friend spoke of a case of a man who came from St. Johns. North Dakota,; where he had been exposed to smallpox. There was nothing to indicate that the man had small-pox or that he would be affected by the disease, yet it is quite true that he might have carried the contagion in his clothes. But no inspection that can be devised. by human ingenuity will enable the officers in every case to detect the person who is carrying the small-pox contagion. The hon. gentleman knows that the period of incubation of the disease is considerable and that even a person who does not develop it may carry the contagion in his clothes and luggage. I appreciate our responsibility as to shutting out disease. We are doing our best in that direction and adopting every means possible. In connection with what the hon. member for Marquette has said I may say that, in no instance where any of the provincial health authorities had given us information that there was danger, have we refused to act on that information. In every case, we have taken steps as promptly as possible to guard against danger. Nor have we always waited for information from the provincial authorities, because my director general of public 'health is in the closest touch with the health authorities of the different frontier states as well as with the Washington authorities, and we are consequently in receipt of information as to the health and the sanitary work of the frontier states. Thus we are advised, perhaps as soon as the provincial authorities, where danger threatens. Wherever danger threatens we appoint an officer. Those officers are appointed temporarily because their services may be needed one month and not the next. The hon. gentleman will agree with me that, in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, where professional services are highly paid. $100 a month is not high for a doctor, even when he is allowed to carry on his own practice as well. If we were to debar these officers from practice, we could not engage them at $100 a month, and probably not at $200 a month, to do this work for the government.
Are these officers supposed to report regularly, or are their duties confined to the time when some particular case of disease is before them?

They are appointed by the month. When we consider that the dan-Mr. ROCHE.
ger at the point on the frontier is past, we notify them that their services are no longer required. While they are on the duty they i ei ort regularly as to the condition of affairs, what they have done and so on.
The minister says they report regularly. Does he mean that they report regularly on cases as they arise, or do they report as a matter of routine at certain intervals ?
They report once a month regularly and of course they report when anything special occurs.

Of course, I cannot criticise the hon. minister, for he has shifted the responsibility with regard to the main question to the Immigration Department. As the cases which do not relate to the hon. gentleman's department were the most flagrant I shall take another opportunity of offering criticism. Some of the municipalities in Manitoba have been put to danger, inconvenience and expense by these cases.
I have no doubt that my colleague the Minister of the Interior when his estimates are under discussion will be able to give full information on the point.
Has the minister got a quarantine officer at Victoria ?
Yes.

I would like to know if the minster's attention has been drawn to an article that appeared in the ' Citizen ' this morning concerning fifteen first-class passengers being quarantined at North Bay. They were passengers from the east. One died on board on the 5th of May. They came up from Victoria to Vancouver where another one was taken sick just thirteen days after the death of the first one, and was taken to the hospital, where it turned out to be a case of small-pox. The other passengers were allowed to come east and were on the train for five days. It does seem to me there must have been carelessness on the part of some person. These people should not have been allowed to land after it was discovered that one person had died on board the ship and another was so bad that he had to be taken to the hospital, and died shortly after landing at Vancouver.
Mr., FISHER. This matter has been brought to my attention although not in this particular form. The steamship ' Athenian ' came from Japan, and was examined at our quarantine station at Victoria. The vessel first touches at Victoria and then goes on to Vancouver. The quarantine station for these incoming Pacific lines is at Victoria. The vessel became a coastwise vessel at Victoria, no disease having been discovered on; board.
That is not what the article says.

Our quarantine officer at Victoria sent a report by letter, and we have had telegraphic communication with him, and he states that he examined the vessel at Victoria on her coming into the quarantine station there and found no disease. He therefore gave her what we call a free pratique, and the vessel then going on to Vancouver became what we call a coastwise vessel, and came under the usual responsibilities of a vessel within the jurisdiction of the province of British Columbia, just as any other vessel going from one port to another port within the province would be. It appears that during that time a case of small-pox developed, and when the vessel arrived in Vancouver she had that case on board. That ease was landed in Vancouver and dealt with by the provincial authorities. The passengers on this vessel were allowed to take the train and come east, and it appears that when some of them arrived in the province of Ontario another case was discovered. It was simply a precaution on the part of the provincial authority of Ontario to hold these people up, because in his judgment they had been in contact with a case of smallpox a short time before. These are briefly the whole facts of the case. As I said a little while ago answering the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) the duty of my department is to examine vessels on arrival at our ports. They are examined with the utmost care and precision, and when no disease is found on these vessels the people are left free to enter the country and then come under the laws of the province in. which they may happen to be. It is the same' on the eastern sea-board. When a vessel arrives from England and touches at Halifax she is examined by the quarantine there, after which she may go on to any other port in Canada. After she has been examined for quarantine she goes forward as a coastwise vessel. When the vessel gets to Quebec she is examined at Grosse Isle at the quarantine station, and goes on to the port of Montreal and is examined again for quarantine, purposes. She is then a vessel in the Dominion of Canada, having passed quarantine at the first port touched, after which she is no longer under our quarantine laws, and we have no longer any control over her or over her passengers.
It seems to be another case of divided authority. I presume that after it leaves the first quarantine station it comes under the control of the Inferior Department.
Not in the case of the * Athenian,' because they were not immigrants.

I do not think it makes much difference whether the people are im- '
migrants or not. When they come to this country and have been exposed to contagious disease, they should come under the control of the quarantine officers. It is a very strange thing that the Dominion officers did not pronounce the disease contagious while the local officers said it was. It is another illustration of how carelessly the machinery for the prevention of that kind of thing is managed in this country. We see every day in the newspapers accounts of people that are landing on our shores who are suffering from various diseases, people who are paupers, and who become a burden on the country. It seems to me there ought to be some way of stopping people, even if they are not immigrants, after they have been exposed to contagious diseases.

My hon. friend must understand that when people come to this country with no appearance of disease about them it would be an unwarrantable interference with liberty to stop them and have them disinfected.
When a man who is so sick that he has to be taken to a hospital, after having been exposed to a contagious disease, is that not a sufficient reason for stopping him ?

So far as the quarantine in concerned we can only deal with contagious diseases. This disease had not developed when the man came to Vancouver and landed there. It was only after he was taken to the hospital in Vancouver that the case was found to be one of small-pox. But when he landed in Victoria he was not recognized as affected with small-pox. It was after that that the case developed into what was called malignant small-pox, and that was after the passengers had landed and were just as free as anybody else to do as they liked. My quarantine officers had absolutely no right in law to detain those passengers. When the vessel passes our quarantine, my officers take no further account of the passengers at all, we let them go, we have no further knowledge of them. No officer of mine knew that this man went to the hospital afterwards.
Has the quarantine officer at Vancouver no authority ?

Not when the vessel has passed the quarantine at Victoria. If a vessel comes to Vancouver without having touched at Victoria my officer at Vancouver deals with her, but if the vessel comes to Victoria and is there given pratique, or clearance, she then becomes a coastwise vessel and my officer at Vancouver deals with her just as a vessel coming to Victoria as if she had not come across the Pacific.

Is it not the duty of the captain of the vessel to report when a man

dies of small-pox on board of his ship and when another man is taken ill just thirteen days after with small-pox, so that the patient may be attended to and put in quarantine ? It does seem to me that it was the captain's duty to have reported that case to your officers.
My hon. friend does not seem to quite grasp the situation.
Perhaps not.
The vessel is dealt with for quarantine purposes according to her papers from her last port of call. This vessel had a clean bill of health.
You will not say that without reference to what occurred on the voyage V

I mean to say that when a vessel from Yokohama conies to Victoria the officers there have no control with anything that may have occurred before she left Yokohama, where the vessel obtained a clean bill of health.
Notwithstanding the fact that a man has died at sea ?
Suppose the disease develops in the meantime ?
Then he deals with it ; but the hon. gentleman is speaking about a case that occurred before the vessel came to Kobe.
That is not a fact.

The hon. gentleman may not know about it, but it is a fact. This was a case of disease that occurred between Nagasaki and Kobe. The vessel at Kobe was thoroughly disinfected by the Japanese authorities, and I may say here that their quarantine work is very effective and thorough. The vessel went on from Kobe to Yokohama and at Yokohama she was given a clean bill of health. Then she came to my quarantine station at Victoria, and the officer's only duty there was to examine the bill of health of the last port of call, which was the port of Yokohama.
Is it not his duty to make an examination of her passengers V
- Certainly, and he did examine her passengers ; but he had nothing to do with what occurred before she left Yokohama.
I understand the minister to say that his only duty was to examine the bill of health given at the last port of call.

What I mean is that his duty, as far as her bill of health was concerned, was only to examine the bill of health given at Yokohama, but he had to examine her passengers. He did examine her passengers. and finding no disease he gave her a Mr. WILSON.
clean bill of health. After she was given that clean bill of health she entered the waters of the Dominion, and after the passengers had arrived in the Dominion a case of small-pox developed. That was only after they had landed at Vancouver. It was not on board the vessel at all. The patient was then in the province of British Columbia, on shore and in a local hospital at Vancouver, entirely out of the control or beyond th j espansibiltty of the quarantine officers. Then the case developed, and the local authorities had to deal with it. Apparently the local authorities did not stop the people who had been in contact with that case before it developed. Some of the passengers who had been on the vessel took the train eastward and came through. The health officer of the province of Ontario thought it advisable to stop them and quarantine them at North Bay, and he did so.
Who will have to pay for that ?
The province of Ontario will have to pay the cost of her own action.
Could the hon. minister state the time that elapsed between the death of the passenger previous to the arrival of the vessel at Yokohama and the time at which this case broke out ?
I am informed that it was over eighteen days. That is from the death of the man on board the vessel until the passengers landed at Vancouver.
Then the vessel was not properly quarantined at Yokohama ?
I cannot say as to that. The usual time of incubation, I understand, is fourteen days.

I think the regulations of the department laid down by the hon. Minister of Agriculture are very unfair indeed to the provincial authorities in those cases where the voyage is technically completed on the arrival of the steamer at the first Canadian port, when it is really not completed until arrival at the second port. The same trouble that has arisen on the Pacific coast has more than once arisen on the Atlantic coast, where steamers have come across the Atlantic and put in at Halifax. After being examined there by the quarantine officer the vessel leaves for St. John, and disease breaks out ou the vessel after it leaves Halifax and before it reaches St. John. Under the regulations laid down by the hon. Minister of Agriculture the quarantine officer in St. John takes no action in regard to that matter at all, and the consequence is that the whole difficulty, trouble and expense are loaded on the province, necessitating two sets of quarantine officers, one set under the control of the provincial authorities and the other under the control of the Dominion authorities. I do not think

it is at all fair to the place where the'voy-age is really concluded to have a regulation of that kind. A vessel may touch at the first port of call merely to discharge mails or passengers, whereas the main port of call is the second place arrived at. I certainly think that the department over which the hon. minister presides ought to make some change in these regulations, so that the voyage will be technically completed where it is really completed-at the port where the vessel is going to and where it discharges and takes on cargo. I am aware that we have had some correspondence between our city and the Department of Agriculture in regard to this matter. This is a question that has created a great deal of friction in our city, because we certainly do think it unfair to throw upon the city of St. John the expense of keeping a quarantine officer to go on board and examine passengers and ships when, under the British North America Act, quarantine is placed under the control of the Dominion authorities. E think, if these are the regulations of the department, it is time they were changed in simple justice to the city authorities where the voyage is completed.

I entirely agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel), because several incidents similar to those which he has referred to have come under my notice. If the Dominion government undertakes quarantine against disease coming from outside it should not take advantage of a technicality when a vessel calls at one port on her way to her destination. I would like to ask my hon. friend if the expenditures that were incurred there were not met by the Department of Marine and Fisheries instead of by the local authorities, as he says ?	,
The expense was met by the city of St. John.
I would like to ask my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) if the communications which he read to the committee to-day were received by him from a medical man ?
The communication sent to me was from the secretary of the provincial board of health, Mr. E. M. Wood.
Is he a medical man ?
No, he is not a medical man.

My hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) wilt readily appreciate that statement that he read to the House must convey the impression that the authorities in that locality are very lax. The hon. member for Marquette being a medical man of good standing himself will agree with me when I say that if the territory to the south of Manitoba was largely infected with smallpox, it would take perhaps 50 nr 75 or 100
medical men along the boundary to guard that province from the invasion of persons with small-pox then on them. But persons who had contracted small-pox a few days before might come in dozens or 'hundreds and yet no number of medical men could be held responsible for an invasion of the disease into Manitoba. I think he will admit that.

I may say that the criticism made by this gentleman was not so much directed to the particular case he refers to along the boundary line except in so far as he had great difficulty in getting any information from the Dominion authorities as to what procedure would be followed in preventing an invasion of small-pox from the United States. He referred more particularly to the influx of Scotch and Ontario immigrants. I presume that Mr. E. M. Wood, who is a very intelligent gentleman and who has been secretary of the Provincial Board of Health for many years, voices the sentiments of the Provincial Board of Health, which is composed of medical men and that he is not doing this off his own bat.

I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) will agree that if they had an intelligent board of health there, there is but one intelligent thing they can do, and that is to vaccinate. Quarantine is all very well as far as it goes, but it is only a very partial preventive against small-pox. There is a divided authority to which the hon. member for St. John has just referred. The quarantine department deals with an invasion of any quarantinable disease from outside the Dominion, but if we have quarantinable diseases occurring on the sea-board in connection with the merchant marine, the officers of the Marine Department have to deal with it, and frequently the question of divided authority is important. I would again suggest that it is very nearly time that arrangements were made whereby quarantinable diseases on the sea-board at least would be dealt with by one department instead of by two departments. I do not know whether the Minister of Agriculture is waiting for recommendations from the medical men of the country or not, but if he is, I think the medical men in this House will secure before the next session recommendations from the various medical bodies throughout Canada to that effect.
There is another matter to which I wish to call his attention. I think that the medical men of Canada would endorse action on the part of the Minister of Agriculture along the line of providing for the establishment of a vaccine station at which medical men could obtain vaccine on which they could rely. We now have to take most of our vaccine from concerns south of the boundary and having had pretty large experience myself in the use of vaccine for some 20 years, I feel safe in saying-and I am sure this will be endorsed by every medical man-that

we feel on many occasions that the vaccine we get is not fresh. This is a matter of very great importance to any locality on the occurrence of the outbreak of small-pox. I would urge that the medical men throughout Canada would endorse the action of the Minister of Agriculture if he took steps to provide a vaccine farm for the benefit of the people.
There are already a number of vaccine farms in Canada. There are two in Ontario, one in Alberta and one in Manitoba.
Are these not all managed by private concerns.
Oh, no, one in Ontario is assisted by the Board of Health and is under its direction.

I am glad my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has brought that to my attention. The providing of good vaccine is so important that we should not leave it in the hands of speculators, for the temptation when a demand is made for large quantities of vaccine is so great that I fear in many cases old and valueless vaeeine would be sent where good vaccine is required. For that reason I hold very strongly that a government vaccine farm should be established, because the medical men of the country would then feel safe in receiving vaccine ; at least they would feel sure that no pecuniary interest precluded them from getting the best.
Have not some requests to that effect already been made to the department ?
The matter has been discussed more or less, but I do not think there has been any request from medical men officially or from any body of men. The question has been up for consideration.

I think it is most unfair to Ontario in these cases which I have brought to the attention of the House that the provincial government should be charged with the quarantining of 15 passengers at North Bay through the carelessness-I do not think that is too strong a word-of the Dominion officials at Vancouver. The regulations may be wrong, but there is one thing certain to my mind, that the officers of either the Department of Agriculture or of the Interior Department, ought to have the power to stop cases of this kind and to prevent people travelling through the country in cars as they please after having been exposed to contagious and dangerous diseases. I consider it is a most unfair thing to the province.

It seems to me there must have been something defective in the examination. I understood the minister to say that all the quarantine officer has to do is to examine the passengers on the vessel Mr. KENDALL.
and look at the clearance at the last place of call. Now, if I understand correctly, he has to go a good deal farther. He has to inquire into any case of sickness that may have taken place on board or any death and to ascertain the nature of the disease. Apparently this was a case of small-pox and the patient had died. Any intelligent quarantine officer knows that the development of small-pox takes so many days after contagion,, and that a vessel might pass one or two ports in the meantime without the incubation having advanced to such an extent that it would be apparent that it was small-pox. If it was brought to his attention that a case had occurred on board and that a patient had died so many days before, it would suggest to him that it was his duty to go further than simply examine the passengers, and if they were apparently in good health allow them to go over the country in any direction.
My hon. friend is quite right, but in this case the criticism does not apply at all. My hon. friend knows that the ordinary period of incubation of small-pox is about 13 or 14 days.
14 days.

Fourteen days. The case the hon. gentleman refers to had occurred before the vessel reached the port of Kobd, and eighteen days elapsed between the time of her leaving that port and the time of her arrival at William's Head, Victoria : so that my officer had no reason for thinking that there could be a development of small-pox from that case which had occurred more than eighteen days before he had examined the vessel and after she had been thoroughly disinfected. The individual passenger who afterwards developed small-pox in Vancouver was carefully examined because he was ill. He showed no signs of small-pox, but he showed signs of sickness from having taken too much alcohol, having been drunk during most of the time he was on board.
How long was it between that time and the time the vessel reached Vancouver ?
I suppose it reached Vancouver the next day.	[DOT]
And a few hours after he reached the hospital the small-pox was out on him ?
He was not taken to the hospital as a small-pox patient. It was after he had got there, I do not know how long after, that the small-pox broke out on him.
Can the minister tell the date of the arrival of the steamship ?
I am not sure of the exact date.

The article in the 'Citizen' says the man died on the 5th of May, and

the other man was taken with the disease on the 18th, which is only thirteen days after.
That is not correct.
The inference is that the ship could not have been properly fumigated at Yokohama.
I cannot say as to that.

Do I understand the minister to say that the examination is made at the first Canadian port at which the vessel touches ? Suppose a vessel is destined for the port of St. John, and she first touches at Halifax, where she is examined and is given a clean bill. If disease develops between Halifax and St. John, which is a run of several hours, does the hon. gentleman mean to say that nothing can be done by the quarantine officers at St. John ?

As a matter of fact, when a vessel comes from England to Halifax, the quarantine officer at Halifax examines it chiefly for the convenience of the ship and the people who land at Halifax ; but the vessel undergoes another examination at St. John, which is a quarantine port. If the vessel were not going to another quarantine port in Canada, the examination at Halifax would be more searching, and the vessel would then be free ; but we have given this concession to the shipowners in order to delay the vessel at Halifax as short a time as possible and have her re-examined at St. John. But the rule is that a vessel shall be examined where she first touches, and after that we have no more responsibility for her.
In case of contagious disease breaking out on a vessel between Halifax and St. John, would the hon. minister's department be liable for the expense ?
It would stop at St. John.
Would you put the case into your own hospital ?
Yes.

I hope that is so. If it is so, I hope the minister will take a different view from the view which has been entertained in his department on one or two occasions. That vessel would be a coastwise vessel, would she not ?
Except in the sense that the examination at Halifax was not a complete examination.
If there were a complete examination at Halifax and a case of disease occurred on the way to St. John, would not the authorities of the Marine and Fisheries Department have to look after the case ?

I do not think the Marine and Fisheries Department would look after the ease when the vessel comes from a for-133
eign port, unless she is under Canadian register.

I think those items are only for the frontier inspection, and have nothing to do with the organized quarantine ports. The expenditure in Quebec ought not to; be under that item at all. It ought to have been under the Grosse Isle quarantine station.

I do not wish to say anything disparaging of the officer in charge of the quarantine station at William's Head, because I think he is eminently qualified to fill the position. The fact is that the ' Athenian ' was given a clean Bill of health at the quarantine station; and after she left the quarantine station and proceeded to Victoria and on to Vancouver, one of the passengers developed some serious illness, was taken fi^the hospital at Vancouver, was found to be suffering from small-pox, from which he died. Although the minister says he died from alcoholic poisoning

No, I said that he had been suffering during the voyage and during the quarantine from too much alcohol, that when he was examined at Victoria by Dr. Watt, he was examined as a sick man. and was therefore more carefully examined than he would have been under ordinary circumstances ; that he was landed at Vancouver as a sick man and was taken to the hospital; that he was not supposed to be affected with contagious disease ; but that some time after he reached the hospital at .Vancouver, he developed small-pox and died.

I beg the honourable gentleman's pardon. I did not quite catch what he said ; but the fact remains that some forty passengers are rounded up in our isolation hospital and have to be kept at the expense of the city of Vancouver. They have to be quarantined in that hospital, as the city cannot afford to have the small-pox spread and be visited again with this terrible scourge which afflicted us ten or twelve years ago. I think that in such a case, when our officers at Williams Head gives a clean bill of health, and a few hours after the disease breaks out and the city is put to considerable expense, the blame should lie at the doors of the quarantine officer, and it is rather unfair that the Dominion government should not recoup the city. I am not saying that our officers are negligent, because I know that Dr.



Watt, who is our quarantine officer at Williams Head, is one of the best men we have. He has done splendid work at that station, and since he has been in charge we have had very little trouble. This is the first instance in which there has been any. It seems to me that the Dominion government should investigate the matter thoroughly and find out if this man had the small-pox when he was examined by the quarantine officer ; and if so, refund the city the expense it was put to.

I have no hesitation in saying that in this individual case, as the facts are reported to me, no possible blame can attach to the quarantine officer at Williams Head. It was quite impossible for him to diagnose the case as small-pox. The question of paying the expenses in Vancouver or elsewhere is a matter of general policy which would have to be settled on general lines. There may be instances where the law may be a little hard, and where perhaps the government might assume the responsibility, but there are many others where it would be very hard to decide. Therefore definite clear lines have been laid down of quarantine responsibility; and when once we begin to doubt, we get into the habit of doing many things which this government should not be called on to do. As far as my own administration is concerned, I must adhere to the clear well-defined lines.

I do not think we can heartily agree in the bon. gentleman's conclusions with regard to this case. To begin with, there was a death from small-pox on board the vessel in question. Of that death there was a record, and the quarantine office must have known it. That in itself should have suggested great care. The officer comes in contact with the sick patient and examines him. We are told that the case was supposed to be one of alcoholic poisoning, but there is no resemblance between that and developed small-pox. The fact that a death from small-pox had occurred should have suggested to the medical man the necessity of ascertaining whether the symptoms in the case before him were not those which might be expected in the development of that disease. There was to say the least some carelessness, or otherwise the medical officer would have been sufficiently suspicious to look for symptoms of the same disease. True the vessel might be disinfected and the clothing, but often articles escape disinfection, which afterwards, when brought into contact with the human body, communicate the infection. There was a case of sickness on board which developed a few hours afterwards into small-pox. It was only a short time from the time the vessel left the quarantine station at Williams Head until she landed at Vancouver, Mr. MACPHERSON.
and immediately on this patient being taken to the hospital, the small-pox was quite apparent. The pustules had developed, which could not have been the case if there had not been symptoms apparent for some time before. Take the temperature, the temperature of a patient suffering from alcoholic poisoning and that of one suffering from small-pox would be different.
His temperature was normal.
It might have been, but I am afraid it would be quite difficult to convince medical men of that.
It is so stated by medical men.
The symptoms must have been apparent when the man was lying ill, and there must have been some carelessness or they would not have escaped notice.

There is what appears to me a weakness in the quarantine regulations which I pointed out on a former occasion. In the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, when a vessel leaves an American port and calls at a Canadian port, she is examined, but when she leaves the Canadian port and then proceeds to another Canadian port, this disease may develop during the voyage. No notice is taken if the disease breaks out after the ship has left one Canadian port and reaches another, the vessel being considered as a coastwise vessel. The hon. minister should look into that and see if the regulations could not be so amended as to meet cases of this kind which may arise any time.
After this man landed in Vancouver, he was examined and found to be suffering from small-pox. Could not the Dominion officer have sent this boat back to quarantine ?
That is not the interpretation put upon the law by the Department of Justice. Once a vessel has got a clear bill of health, we have no authority over it.
After having been examined at Williams Head and after she had reached Victoria, the disease broke out.

The examination takes place between Williams Head and Victoria. It finishes just as she goes to Victoria. The doctor goes on board and frequently goes to Victoria with the ship. And, if he does keep her there, it is only for a couple of hours till she reaches the wharf at Victoria. Williams Head and Victoria are one port.

In the supposititious case, this vessel does not call at Victoria, but will go direct to Vancouver. After having passed Williams Head upon

going to Vancouver, she is not a coastwise vessel until she reaches Vancouver. It is a hardship to Vancouver that the regulations should be as they are. As a matter of fact this disease is brought in by a foreign vessel and landed on our shores in Vancouver. In the particular case that has been referred to, I do not think there is any possible chance of the disease spreading. But the fact of these people coming in causes the city of Vancouver to be put to very heavy expense. My impression is that the quarantine regulations should be such that, if any disease develops within fourteen days after the arrival of a vessel at quarantine, the Dominion government should be responsible, because the fact that it develops in that time proves that it was on the vessel.
Is there any person who can tell us how the fifteen passengers got away that were reported to be in quarantine at Vancouver ?

I would like to set the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) right about that. After the disease had broken out and the patient had died, our authorities in Vancouver rounded up all the passengers who had been on the boat and who were in the city. Of course, they had been going about the streets for three or four days. They have got them isolated now.

I notice that some of the hon. gentleman's officials are paid $100 a month while others are paid $150 a month. In some of the border towns, where apparently, 'there would be more work to do in connection with quarantine, the pay is only $100 while, for instance, Dr. Tyerman, of Prince Albert, received $150. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) will find it at page D-0(5 of the Auditor General's Report-salary for June, 1902, $150 and expenses $120.

I can only say that the payments to Dr. Tyerman were made on Dr. Patterson initialling and authorizing the account. I cannot state now the reason why in this case $150 was paid, unless this gentleman had to be in constant attendance on some case at $5 per day for a month. In the cases the hon. gentleman refers to of officers on the frontier, these are appointed at a stated salary. These officers are appointed from here. But in other cases, Dr. Patterson is authorized to make what arrangements he can and he must initial all accounts.
I see that Dr. Hughes has been paid $100 a month for a certain portion, and from 1st April to June 30th, $200 a month. Why was that?

I am informed that Dr. Hughes, during part of the time, was absent from home being sent down to the frontier, and he would not go for less than this salary. We could not get any other man, so we sent him. It was a temporary matter.

1 do not know whether
the minister has explained what seems an excessive charge for Dr. Patterson. I see charges $20 a day. That is as much as a cabinet minister receives.
But my hon. friend (Mr. Rosamond) will see that it is not a yearly salary, but is paid for 250 days. When the arrangement was made it was expected that it would be for a short time.
Dr. Patterson gets not only $20 a day, but living expenses as well. This puts him in a better position than a cabinet minister who receives only $7,000.
Oh, we are not in it with these professional men.

The director general only gets $4,000 a year which is much less in proportion to wliat this quarantine officer receives. I would like to know why Dr. Patterson is paid what seems to me an excessive salary ?

I do not believe we could get a medical man who would take the responsibility and do the work at less than $20 a day. I confess that it seems to me to be a high rate, but I find that professional men, lawyers and doctors, insist on high salaries when paid by the day.
